quotes.text: Analytical investigations for this problem lead to the development of a heuristic that is proved to be asymptotically optimal under standard assumptions about the problem parameters.
The approach contrasts and complements the current practice in process systems engineering, which is entirely empirical in nature.

title: The assignment problem with external interactions
contribution: Defines APEX (assignment with a single unrestricted arc) and gives a sequential shortest path algorithm that needs far less storage and runs 2 to 52 times faster than network flow and assignment codes (abstract).
problem_entry: Assignment extended to divert internal jobs outside and accept external ones: a linear assignment problem with one unrestricted arc (abstract).
key_idea: Initialization heuristics give a dual feasible, complementary-slack partial assignment; shortest augmenting paths complete it (abstract).
experiments: Compared with state-of-the-art network flow and assignment codes on APEX's exact reformulations; much smaller storage, 2 to 52 times faster (abstract).
positioning: Benchmarked against general network flow and assignment approaches (abstract).
transferable: Benchmark a special-structure algorithm against the general codes run on exact reformulations of the same instances, and report memory as well as speed (abstract).

quotes.text: As APEX can be formulated as a minimum-cost network flow problem and as a standard assignment problem of larger size, we compare the proposed algorithm with state-of-the-art network flow and assignment approaches.
In addition, extensive computational results demonstrate that it is from 2 to 52 times faster.

title: Robust process planning under uncertainty
contribution: Adds a robustness measure that penalizes second-stage costs above their expectation to two-stage stochastic process planning while keeping the model linear (abstract).
problem_entry: Two-stage stochastic programs ignore the variability of second-stage costs and can return plans with unacceptably high realized costs (abstract).
key_idea: Penalize second-stage costs above the expected cost; no nonlinearities are introduced, so LP techniques solve large instances (abstract).
assumptions: Two-stage stochastic programming: decisions before and after the uncertain parameters are revealed (abstract).
limits_future: Specialized models and solution schemes for process networks are announced but not described in the abstract (abstract).

method_links.note: LP-first stance applied to the model rather than a relaxation: the robustness measure keeps the formulation linear so large instances stay LP-solvable.

transferable: Add risk aversion to a two-stage stochastic program with a penalty on second-stage costs above their expectation, which keeps the deterministic equivalent linear (abstract).

quotes.text: A potential limitation of this approach is that it does not account for the variability of the second-stage costs and might lead to solutions where the actual second-stage costs are unacceptably high.

Incorporating this measure into stochastic programming formulations does not introduce nonlinearlities, thus making possible the solution of large-scale problems through linear programming techniques.

title: A finite algorithm for global minimization of separable concave programs
contribution: A finite branch-and-bound algorithm with domain reduction for separable concave programs, with a finiteness guarantee for every exhaustive rectangular branch-and-bound that branches on the incumbent (abstract).
problem_entry: Separable concave programming, one of the earliest branches of nonlinear programming, studied for over thirty years (abstract).
key_idea: Find the exact global minimum in finitely many iterations, accelerated by domain reduction (abstract).
proof_devices: finiteness proof extended to all branch-and-bound algorithms for concave programming that partition exhaustively with rectangles and branch on the incumbent when possible (abstract)
experiments: Up to 100 nonlinear and 400 linear variables and 50 constraints in about five minutes on an IBM RS/6000; an industrial case with 152 nonlinear and 593 linear variables and 417 constraints in about ten minutes (abstract).
writing: Opens with the problem's thirty-year history before the claim (abstract).

method_links.note: Domain reduction techniques are the named accelerator of the finite algorithm.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: finite branching by exhaustiveness plus incumbent branching
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Source paper of the rule: finiteness for every rectangular branch-and-bound that partitions exhaustively and branches on the incumbent (restated by H010, S058, S077 in s01).

transferable: Make a rectangular branch-and-bound finite for concave minimization by combining exhaustive partitioning with branching at the incumbent, and prove the guarantee for the algorithm family, not only for your code (abstract).

quotes.text: In addition to proving that our algorithm terminates finitely, the paper extends a guarantee of finiteness to all branch-and-bound algorithms for concave programming that (1) partition exhaustively using rectangular subdivisions and (2) branch on the incumbent solution when possible.

The algorithm uses domain reduction techniques to accelerate convergence; it solves problems with as many as 100 nonlinear variables, 400 linear variables and 50 constraints in about five minutes on an IBM RS/6000 Power PC.

probabilistic analysis: heuristic error vanishes asymptotically with probability one (abstract)
experiments: Computational results to substantiate the theory; no details in the abstract (abstract).

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Approximation scheme whose error vanishes with probability one as problem size grows.

quotes.text: By means of a computational complexity analysis, we first prove that the general process planning problem is NP-hard, and thus efficient exact algorithms for this class of problems are unlikely to exist.

Subsequently, we develop an approximation scheme for this problem and prove, via probabilistic analysis, that the error of the heuristic vanishes asymptotically with probability one as the problem size increases.

quotes.text: Using the notion of a generating set, we establish conditions under which the tightest convex extension is the convex envelope.
